ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry Referral — Jean-Jacques Rousseau — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit for beliefs of being plotted against, poor sleep, and difficulty passing urine

text.paragraph: Fixed beliefs for some nine years that former friends and colleagues are coordinating a campaign to ruin him, worse over the past year, with insomnia, in a 54-year-old writer. Please assess the diagnosis and the risk to himself and others, and advise on treatment and on his capacity to consent to urethral surgery. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks; no current suicidal or violent ideation. [S]

list.item: Is this delusional disorder, persecutory type, or does it fit paranoid personality disorder, schizophrenia, a mood disorder with psychotic features, or a medical or neurocognitive cause better? Is brain imaging needed?
What is his risk of suicide and of violence toward the people he believes are persecuting him, and is outpatient care safe?
Should an antipsychotic be offered, which one given his urinary retention, and how should it be discussed with a man who does not see himself as ill?
Is cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis suitable, and how should we engage him without confronting the beliefs?
Does he have the capacity to consent to urethral surgery, and are there perioperative psychiatric considerations?

text.paragraph: He believes that former friends, publishers, and the people around him are working together to defame him and are opening his letters and messages. He holds this with full conviction, has stopped opening letters from people he suspects, and sleeps about four hours. He has real public conflicts over his books, and a previous home abroad was attacked with stones. No hallucinations; no substance use beyond a glass of wine a few times a week; no previous psychiatric treatment. Mental status: guarded but courteous, logical, anxious, non-bizarre persecutory beliefs, no suicidal or violent ideation, no firearms. MoCA 28; PHQ-9 8 (item 9 scored 0); GAD-7 9; blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, TSH, and vitamin B12 normal; neurological examination normal. He also has lifelong difficulty passing urine, treated for years by self-dilation with urethral sounds; maximum flow 6.2 mL/s, residual 180 mL, and urethral imaging and cystoscopy are booked; urethroplasty is a likely option. He has a small right inguinal hernia. No medicines; no known allergy. He distrusts doctors, wants to read his own records, and has declined permission for us to speak with anyone else. A safety plan and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline are in place [S]

list.item: Cannot pass urine freely: a thin stream, straining, burning, and the feeling of never emptying; fears the passage will one day close completely; dilates himself with urethral sounds every few days. [S]
Sleeps four hours a night and lies awake going over what his former friends are doing to his name. [S]
Wants to be believed and not called mad, to read his own records, and to decide for himself; has little trust in doctors. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva on June 28, 1712. Geneva had followed the Gregorian calendar since 1701, so the date needs no conversion. [D]
His mother, Suzanne Bernard, died nine days after his birth. [D]

In the Confessions he wrote that a defect in the bladder caused him an almost continual retention of urine in his early years; that he reached thirty almost without feeling this original infirmity, apart from frequent heats in the bladder; that burning and pain in the loins returned at Venice; and that after a hot summer of journeys on foot he had a violent nephritic colic, after which he never recovered his former health. [D]

In the Confessions he wrote that the surgeon Morand advised him to go to Daran, whose bougies were the only ones that gave him any relief; he bought a great number of them so that he would never be without, and used them often for eight or ten years. [D]

His letters show that he spoke of urinary retention from 1748, at 36. In 1761 a probe broke in his urethra and he feared it would cost him his life; he wrote that he could not stop using his probes for a single day and that he had carried a bladder disease since childhood. A surgeon, Brother Côme, succeeded in passing a probe and ruled out a stone. [D]

He described his trouble as a habitual state: he never passed urine with a full stream, the flow was never wholly stopped, and he judged that the stream grew thinner from year to year and would one day stop altogether. [D]
In 1758 he suffered frequent retentions together with a rupture, and passed the year in a state of languor that made him think he was near the end of his life. [D]
In a will dated January 29, 1763, he asked that his body be opened after death, to show that his urinary disorder did not come from a dissolute life. [D]
By his own account in the Confessions he had five children with Thérèse Levasseur, and all five were taken to the foundling hospital shortly after birth. [D]

His books were condemned in 1762; stones were thrown at his house at Môtiers in September 1765; and he came to England in January 1766 at the invitation of a Scottish philosopher. He lived at Wootton, in the parish of Ellastone in rural Staffordshire, from March 22, 1766, to May 1, 1767, in a house belonging to Richard Davenport, and wrote the first part of the Confessions there. [D]

In England he became wrongly convinced that the Scottish philosopher who had arranged his stay was at the center of a plot against him, and he feared that the servants were spying on him. The two men quarreled violently, and the 1911 Britannica called his letters of this time those of a lunatic. [D]

The French psychiatrists Sérieux and Capgras classed him among patients with a delusion of interpretation, and a 2023 history-of-medicine paper judges that by current criteria he had a paranoid delusion that appeared around the age of 45 and grew afterwards, while noting that he had real enemies and real persecution (his books condemned, and expulsion by the Swiss authorities). [R]

The cause of his urinary disorder is disputed. Proposed causes include a congenital narrowing of the urethra (Poncet and Leriche, and his own phrase, a defect of conformation), a stricture of the penile urethra (judged most probable in a 2023 paper), a muscular valve at the bladder neck (Mercier), urinary retention of psychological origin (Janet), and acute intermittent porphyria (Androutsos and Geroulanos, 2000). [R]

He distrusted the medicine of his time: in Emile he wrote that he would never call a physician for himself unless his life were in evident danger, and in the Confessions he wrote that the physicians he consulted gave him no relief and weakened him. [D]
In a letter he wrote that when snow and frost shut him in he split wood to make himself sweat twice a day, the only remedy that had ever given him the least relief. [D]

Weak urinary stream, straining, incomplete emptying (post-void residual 180 mL), and painful urination since childhood, treated for years by self-dilation with urethral sounds; cause not yet established; urethral imaging and endoscopy booked: active, confirmed [S]
Right inguinal hernia, reducible and minimally symptomatic, likely aggravated by years of straining to pass urine: active, confirmed [S]

Engagement without confrontation: listen to his account in full, acknowledge his distress and the real conflicts in his life, neither argue with nor agree with the beliefs, and agree shared goals that matter to him (sleep, less distress, freedom to write, and his bladder); give him copies of his results and notes. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, Third Edition. Am J Psychiatry 2020;177(9):868-872 (2020); Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR): delusional disorder (2022) [S]

Look for medical, substance, and neurocognitive causes: neurological examination, MoCA, blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, TSH, and vitamin B12; review of medicines and alcohol; brain imaging only if the course or examination is atypical. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, Third Edition. Am J Psychiatry 2020;177(9):868-872 (2020); Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR): delusional disorder (2022) [S]

Structured suicide and violence risk assessment with a written safety plan and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; no firearms in the home; risk reviewed at every visit; signs for urgent care written down with him. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024) [S]

Urology assessment: IPSS, uroflowmetry, bladder scan for post-void residual, urinalysis, and creatinine now, and kidney and bladder ultrasound this week; retrograde urethrogram, voiding cystourethrogram, and flexible cystoscopy by the urology team next week; stop self-dilation with urethral sounds (urethral rest) and come in the same day if he cannot pass urine. Guideline: Urethral Stricture Disease: AUA Guideline Amendment (2023). Wessells H, et al. J Urol 2023;210(1):64-71. PMID 37096574 (2023) [S]

Right inguinal hernia: watchful waiting while it is minimally symptomatic, with the warning signs of incarceration explained; reassess once the straining has been relieved. Guideline: International guidelines for groin hernia management. HerniaSurge Group. Hernia 2018;22(1):1-165 (2018) [S]

Sleep: fixed rising time, daylight walks, no writing about his enemies after 8 pm, and no sedating antihistamines or anticholinergic sleep aids, which can worsen urinary retention. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, Third Edition. Am J Psychiatry 2020;177(9):868-872 (2020); Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR): delusional disorder (2022) [S]
Referral to psychiatry, Ambrose Lindqvist-Hale, MD, ordered 1767-01-20 [S]
